accuracy.evidence: Checked against the DfE English programmes of study (2013) English Appendix 2 glossary: determiner types (articles the/a/an, demonstratives this/those, possessives my/your, quantifiers some/every, numbers), the note that many words are determiners before a noun and pronouns alone, a/an by first sound (an hour, a unicorn, a one-off), possessive pronouns mine/yours/hers with no apostrophe, and adverbials as words, phrases or clauses saying when, where or how. Year 4 terminology list matches; Common Core L.1.1d and L.1.1h cited.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the main errors directly: apostrophes in your's/her's (step 4 offers my's as a trap and explains why), a/an chosen by letter (hour, unicorn, umbrella in step 2 with a predict), assuming this/some are always determiners (step 3 sort), and calling my a pronoun (adult note plus label step). Each also has a practice or mastery item.

lab_distinct.evidence: New lab flagdetpro: tag chips with arrows from each determiner to its noun, a/an picker by sound, determiner-vs-pronoun sort, my-to-mine builder and a four-label sentence parser. Shingle similarity is at most 3.6% vs flag_tense.js and 3.0% vs any other flag lab, well under the 30% gate.

lab_teaches.evidence: Every step acts out the one test the lesson teaches: does a noun come next? Tagged determiners draw an arrow to their noun, a/an says the word aloud and names the first sound, the sort cards show the following word, and the final label step puts determiner, pronoun, possessive pronoun and adverbial together in one sentence.

predictions.evidence: Three predict prompts before the action: how many determiners are in 'my sister' style phrases, whether 'a hour' or 'an hour' is right before hearing the rule, and whether 'this' in 'I want this.' is a determiner or pronoun; each reveals the answer with a reason after the child commits.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The challenge asks mixed questions (e.g. which word is a determiner in 'Every child got a sticker') and wrong taps get a why() reason naming the word class. In a phone probe, tapping 'red' gave 'red is an adjective. It describes. The determiner comes first: a red.' and 'my's' gave 'No apostrophe! Possessive pronouns never take one: mine.'

readability.evidence: Kid explanation measured at Flesch-Kincaid grade 1.8 (target 5.0) with short sentences and concrete examples (the dog, my bag, I want this); adult explanation 7.3 (target 10.0). Key terms are exact Year 4 vocabulary and each is defined on first use with an example.

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph carries a rule plus an example: the determiner list, the a/an sound rule with hour/unicorn, the 'does a noun come next' test, and the no-apostrophe rule. Explanation overlap with other lessons is under 1% (0.8% vs Linking paragraphs with adverbials) and the filler regex gate passed.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots on an iPhone 13 viewport in light and dark show large chips and bins that fit without sideways scrolling; every action works by tap-then-tap as well as drag, and walk.cjs completed all five Show-me tasks plus the challenge on phone and desktop with no console errors.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark theme on desktop and phone. Every chip, bin and answer is a real button, the canvas has a live aria-label describing the current task and state, and the visual sorter uses text labels rather than colour alone.
